title: Mini project 1: school library lending system
specPoints: 2.1.1–2.1.2 Decomposition, structure diagrams, designing and refining algorithms
2.2.1–2.2.3 Sequence, selection, iteration, string manipulation, 2D lists, file handling, sub programs
2.3.1–2.3.2 Validation, maintainability, test plans with normal/boundary/invalid/erroneous data; Practical programming skills (Section B)
learn: Turn a nine-requirement brief into a numbered checklist, a data design and a structure diagram
Build a file-backed, menu-driven program in three staged steps, testing after each
Implement search (partial, case-insensitive), borrow, return, overdue report and add
Write and run a test plan covering every requirement with all four data types
Evaluate the finished program requirement by requirement with test evidence
hook: A school library with 600 books still uses a paper book to record loans. The librarian wants a program by Friday. She has written exactly what it must do — nine things. This is the walk-through project: you will build it in three steps with help at every stage, so that in the next two projects you can do it with less, and then none.

video.title: Walk-through: the library system in three steps
video.brief: 5 minutes. The brief with its nine requirements numbered. The record design `[id, title, author, borrower, due]` and the file. Structure diagram. Step 1: load, show all, menu — run, four books listed. Step 2: search, borrow, return — borrow book 1, due day appears; try to borrow it again, 'already out'. Step 3: overdue report for day 15 shows Wonder and Noughts and Crosses; add a book, id 7 appears; quit, file updated. End: the nine requirements ticked against a test plan.

explain.h: The brief and the requirements checklist
p: Read it twice, then number. Each requirement is worth marks in the way a Section B question is: addressed visibly or not at all.
explain.code:
BRIEF: A school library needs a program to manage book loans.

R1  Load the books from books.txt when the program starts.                      [1]
R2  Show a validated menu repeatedly until the user chooses Quit.                [1]
R3  Show all books with their status (in, or out to whom and due when).          [1]
R4  Search for books by title; any part of the title, ignoring case.             [2]
R5  Borrow a book by its id: only if it is in; record the borrower's name         [2]
    and the due day (today + 14).
R6  Return a book by its id: only if it is out; clear the borrower and due day.   [1]
R7  Overdue report: ask for today's day number and list all books whose          [2]
    due day is before today, with the borrower's name.
R8  Add a new book with the next unused id, title and author (not blank).        [1]
R9  Save the books to books.txt after every change and on quit.                  [1]
    All input validated; the program must never crash on bad input.             [1]
                                                                        Total [13]

p: Nouns: book, id, title, author, borrower, due day, file. One **record** per book as a list of five fields; an empty borrower string means the book is in. Days are whole numbers (day of term) so no date library is needed. Index constants (`ID = 0`, `TITLE = 1` …) make `b[BORROWER]` readable instead of `b[3]` — a maintainability choice you should copy.
explain.code:
Record:  [id, title, author, borrower, due]
          int  str    str     str ("" if in)  int (0 if in)

File (books.txt), one record per line, fields separated by commas:
1,Holes,Louis Sachar,,0
2,Wonder,R J Palacio,Ada,14

List of lists:
books = [[1, "Holes", "Louis Sachar", "", 0],
         [2, "Wonder", "R J Palacio", "Ada", 14], ...]

p: Verbs: load, show, search, borrow, return, report, add, save. Each is a function; `find_book` and `format_book` are helpers that several of them share. Build in three steps and **run after each**: Step 1 load + show all + menu loop (R1, R2, R3). Step 2 search + borrow + return (R4, R5, R6). Step 3 overdue + add + save (R7, R8, R9). Validation comes free from `get_int`/`get_text` if you use them for every input.
explain.code:
Library system
        ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
   load_books          menu loop               save_books
            ┌─────┬──────┬──────┬────────┬──────┐
        show_all search borrow return  overdue  add
                   └──────┴──────┘
                  use find_book, format_book

explain.h: Three decisions worth making before you type
list: **Search**: `if text.lower() in b[TITLE].lower()` gives partial, case-insensitive matching in one line. Print every match; print 'No matches' if none.

**Borrow/return state**: a book is in when `b[BORROWER] == ""`. Borrow must refuse if it is out; return must refuse if it is in. That is two selection statements with clear messages — and two test rows each.
**Next id**: the largest existing id plus one, or 1 if the list is empty. Do not use `len(books) + 1` — after a deletion it could repeat an id.

p: Nine things the library program must do. Number them. Each one is marks. Build them in three steps.
One book = `[id, title, author, borrower, due]`. Borrower is `""` when the book is in. One line per book in `books.txt`.

list: Step 1: load, show all, menu. Run it.
Step 2: search, borrow, return. Run it.
Step 3: overdue report, add, save. Run it.

keyterms.def: The brief rewritten as numbered things the program must do, used to plan, build, test and evaluate.
A named constant for a position in a record, e.g. `TITLE = 1`, so `b[TITLE]` reads clearly.
A search that succeeds when the search text appears anywhere inside the field.
The current condition of a record, e.g. a book being in or out, decided here by whether the borrower is blank.
Output produced by selecting and formatting records that meet a condition, e.g. all overdue books.
Building a program in planned steps, running and testing after each, rather than all at once.

try.title: Step 1 — load, show all, menu (R1, R2, R3)
p: The helpers, file handling, `find_book` and `format_book` are given — read them first, especially `format_book`. Complete `show_all` and `show_menu`, and make the main loop call `show_all` for option 1. Run: option 1 must list six books with their status; invalid choices must be rejected; 8 quits. Nothing else needs to work yet.

p: Step 1 is done for you here. Complete the three functions following the docstrings and the lesson's decisions. Then test, in this order: search `the` (expect The Hobbit **and** Northern Lights — look at Nor-the-rn; partial matching has surprises), search `HOLES` (expect Holes), search `zzz` (No matches); borrow 1 as `Mo` on day 10 (due 24); borrow 1 again (already out); borrow 99 (no such book); return 1; return 1 again (not out).

try.title: Test plan and evaluation
p: Write the test plan **before** your final run — at least 16 rows, at least one per requirement, every input with a boundary and an erroneous row. Suggested boundary rows: overdue on the exact due day; borrow with id equal to the highest id; add when the list is empty (delete the file contents first). Run it all on your Step 3 program. Log and fix failures. Then write the evaluation table (R1–R9 + validation: met/partly/not, test evidence, next step) and three sentences on robustness, maintainability and one limitation.
steps: Common failures to look for: search matching the author instead of the title; borrowing a book that is out; overdue using `<=` so books due today appear; `next_id` using `len(books) + 1`.

Your evaluation must mention one thing the brief did **not** say that a real librarian would want (a borrower's loan limit? renewals?) — and say you did not build it. That is honest scoping, not failure.

try.title: Save the project
instructions: Save your finished Step 3 program as `library.py`, with `books.txt` beside it, your test plan as `library_tests.txt` and the evaluation as `library_evaluation.txt`.
At the top of `library.py` paste the nine requirements as comments and write the function name that meets each one beside it.

check.q: In the record design, a book is 'in' when:
check.fb: Blank borrower means nobody has it.

check.q: Case-insensitive partial title search is best written as:
check.fb: Lower both sides, then `in` for any part.

check.q: A book due on day 14 is checked on day 14. It should appear in the overdue report:
opts: Only if the borrower is Ada
check.fb: The brief says 'before today'; 14 is a boundary that tests the comparison.

check.q: The next id for a new book should be:
check.fb: After a deletion, `len + 1` could repeat an id.

check.q: R9 says save after every change. The simplest way to meet it is:
opts: Open the file in append mode in each function
Call `save_books` at the end of borrow, return and add
check.fb: One call after each change keeps the file in step.

exam.q: Write a function `countOut(books)` that returns the number of books currently on loan. Each book is stored as `[id, title, author, borrower, due]` and the borrower field is an empty string when the book is in.
model: Function header with the parameter and a counter set to 0 (1). Loop through every book testing whether the borrower field is not empty, incrementing the counter (1). Counter returned after the loop (1).
exam.commentary: Write question. Testing `due > 0` is also accepted because the design sets due to 0 when in. Returning inside the loop loses the last mark.

exam.q: The librarian now wants the borrow option to refuse a loan if the borrower already has 3 books out. Describe how the program would be refined to meet this, naming the data checked and where the check goes.
model: Count the books whose borrower field equals the name entered (1) — in `borrow_book` after the name is entered and before the record is changed (1); if the count is 3 or more print a refusal and do not set borrower/due (1).
exam.commentary: Refine/design question answerable in English. 'Add a check' alone scores nothing; what is counted, where, and what happens are the three marks.

exam.q: Give **two** items of test data for the overdue report when a book is due on day 20, stating the type of each and the expected result.
model: Today = 20: boundary (1), book not listed (1). Today = 21 (or any later day): normal (1), book listed with borrower (1). Also accepted: today = 19 normal, not listed; 'twenty' erroneous, rejected and asked again.
exam.commentary: Value, type and expected result. The boundary row is the one that catches `<=` — students who only give 'day 30' have not tested the edge.

home: Finish the test plan and evaluation if they are not done. Then refine: make the overdue report also show how many days overdue each book is, add the test rows for it, and update the evaluation.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 2 · explain 10 · Step 1: 10 · Step 2: 15 · Step 3: 13 · test plan and evaluation 8 · homework 2. If the class is slower, Step 3 and the evaluation can run into a second lesson; do not shorten the test plan.
misconceptions: Searching with `==` so only the whole title matches, or searching the author field.
Borrow that overwrites an existing borrower because the 'is it in?' check is missing.
Overdue report using `<=` — the boundary row (today equals due) catches it.
Saving only on quit, so a crash loses every loan made in the session (R9).
say: 'Run after Step 1. Six books on screen? Then Step 2.'
'Which requirement number does that function meet? Write it in the docstring.'
'Book due day 14, today day 14. Overdue or not? Test it.'
teacher.skip: Nothing. If time is short, Step 3's `add_book` can be homework, but the overdue report (the only report in the brief) and the test plan must be done in class.
differentiation: Support: students work on Step 2 and Step 3 only, using the given completed code for the earlier steps; pair the weakest with the test plan task first so they know what the program must do.
Stretch: after Step 3, implement the 3-book loan limit from exam question 2 and a 'renew' option that adds 14 days to the due day if the book is out and not overdue.
